title: Miss X Versus Late Rekha Waghmare: The Selective Outrage of Telangana Civil Society
content:
In Telangana, the term “civil society” evokes images of principled activism: women’s groups marching for justice, human rights organisations amplifying marginalised voices, and political parties channelling public anger into demands for accountability. Yet this activism reveals a troubling selectivity when the victim belongs to a Scheduled Caste (SC) community, especially a vulnerable migrant labourer. The stark contrast between the high-profile handling of the Miss X POCSO case and the alleged gang-rape and murder of Late Rekha Waghmare exposes what can only be described as caste-driven hypocrisy. Telangana’s so-called civil society functions less as a beacon of universal justice and more as a caste society indifferent, even complicit, when atrocities target SC “untouchable” communities.

The Miss X Case: Swift Action, Political Storm, and Current Legal Position

In May 2026, Bandi Sai Bhageerath, son of Union Minister of State for Home Affairs Bandi Sanjay Kumar, faced serious criminal allegations under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act and relevant sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). The complaint, lodged on May 8, 2026, by the mother of Miss X, a 17-year-old girl, accused him of repeated sexual harassment, assault, emotional manipulation, and coercive acts over several months at various locations, including a farmhouse in Moinabad.

Despite his father’s prominent political standing, the initial state machinery moved with noticeable readiness. Following an intense police manhunt and the issuance of a lookout notice, Telangana police arrested Bhageerath on May 16, 2026. He was remanded to judicial custody, subjected to custodial police interrogation, and the investigation proceeded swiftly amidst massive public scrutiny. Protests erupted across Hyderabad and throughout the state; women’s groups, student organisations, and opposition parties (including BRS, CPI, and others) staged aggressive dharnas and demonstrations demanding accountability and an impartial Special Investigation Team (SIT) probe. The media covered every twist and turn relentlessly, ensuring that political patronage could not quietly bury the case.

Regarding the latest position in the case, after spending over 50 days in judicial detention, Bandi Sai Bhageerath approached the Telangana High Court seeking regular bail. On July 9, 2026, Justice K. Sujana of the Telangana High Court granted him regular bail subject to strict conditions. Following his release on bail, Bhageerath moved the High Court seeking orders to restrain social media platforms and mainstream media outlets from publishing defamatory content or reporting prejudicial material concerning the POCSO case, in which the High Court subsequently passed interim restraining directions and sought counter-affidavits from the respondents. While the prosecution’s trial process and chargesheet proceedings continue under the statutory oversight of the special POCSO court, the case stands out as a prime instance where public mobilisation, political contention, and intense civil society pressure forced law enforcement to register the FIR promptly, arrest a powerful minister’s son, and hold custodial interrogation.

The Late Rekha Waghmare Case: Systemic Silence, Cover-Up, and Institutional Apathy.

At roughly the same time, an appalling horror unfolded in Donkeshwar village, Nandipet Mandal, Nizamabad district. Late Rekha Waghmare, a 32-year-old Scheduled Caste woman and migrant agricultural labourer hailing from Patoda Khurd village in Dharmabad Taluka, Nanded district, Maharashtra, was found dead under highly suspicious circumstances on the afternoon of February 13, 2026.

Since 2021, Rekha and her husband, Devidas Waghmare, along with their two young daughters (Jeevika, aged 10, and Sona, aged 8), had been living in a small shed on the agricultural land of a local influential landlord, Barla Narsing Reddy, working on a salaried labour basis. According to the consistent representations submitted by Rekha’s brother-in-law, Sri S. Sanjeev, the landlord had repeatedly harassed Rekha and attempted to exploit her. On February 13, 2026, Narsing Reddy intentionally sent Devidas away to work at another distant agricultural plot with strict orders not to return until all work was finished. The children were away at school. Taking advantage of Rekha being completely alone, Barla Narsing Reddy and his associate, Vittal Empalwad (or Emphalwar), allegedly broke into the house, overpowered her, and brutally gang-raped her. When she resisted and attempted to flee, they allegedly murdered her, arranged her body to pretend a hanging, and staged a suicide. They then summoned Devidas, broke down the door in his presence, took photographs, and concocted a story that she had died by suicide.

Instead of initiating a rigorous homicide and sexual assault investigation, the local Nandipet police acted in overt collusion with influential village figures. As detailed in formal representations, police constables Shabir and Vijay, acting alongside a local influential individual named Bharat Reddy, hurried the deceased woman’s body away to the hospital before a formal inquest or inspection by the Sub-Inspector could be conducted. Taking gross advantage of the fact that the grieving family members were non-native Marathi speakers unfamiliar with the Telugu script, the Nandipet police drafted a manipulated Telugu complaint and obtained signatures from Rekha’s 70-year-old father, Meesaye Gangadhar Maadhu. Consequently, Nandipet Police registered FIR No. 33/2026 only under Section 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) for abetment of suicide—shockingly naming Rekha’s own husband, Devidas Waghmare, as the sole accused, while completely shielding the real perpetrators, Barla Narsing Reddy and Vittal Empalwad.

Glaring Forensic Evidence Contradicting the Suicide Theory

The official post-mortem examination (PME No. 103/2026 dated 14.02.2026, conducted at Government Medical College / Government General Hospital, Nizamabad) revealed damning physical findings that directly destroy the suicide narrative:

Severe Antemortem Head Injury: A massive 8 x 4 cm contusion was recorded over the left parietotemporal region of her scalp, accompanied by underlying subdural haemorrhage over the left frontotemporal region of the brain. This severe blunt-force trauma to the head is completely incompatible with an ordinary hanging and remains entirely unexplained by the police suicide theory.

Absence of Vital Reaction in Ligature Mark: The neck examination noted a pressure abrasion (25 x 2-3 cm) obliquely situated above the thyroid cartilage. Dissection revealed that the subcutaneous tissue under the ligature mark was whitened, hardened, and glistening without extravasation of blood in and around, while the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage remained intact. The absence of vital bleeding reactions strongly indicates that the ligature was applied when the victim was in an entirely non-responsive, incapacitated state, ranging from deep unconsciousness to complete biological death—a classic medical hallmark of homicidal violence staged as hanging

Defensive Injuries: The autopsy documented distinct abrasions measuring 2 x 1 cm on the back of the left arm and 3 x 2 cm on the back of the right elbow, pointing to defensive struggle against violent physical assault. Subsequent Regional Forensic Science Laboratory (RFSL) Kamareddy reports confirmed that no poisonous substance was found in the viscera (File No: RFSL/KMR/TOX/104/2026, dated 17.03.2026). While seminal stains were not detected on vaginal/anal swabs (File No: RFSL/KMR/SER/11/2026, dated 02.03.2026), the presence of massive blunt intracranial trauma and defensive abrasions undeniably established homicidal foul play.

The Institutional Wall: Closure by SPCA and Continued Harassment of the Bereaved Family

Faced with deliberate police sabotage, the victim’s family, assisted by an advocate pursued remedies across every institutional channel. Formal representations demanding reinvestigation, addition of gang-rape and murder charges under BNS (Sections 64, 70/66, 103) and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, and the constitution of a Special Investigation Team (SIT) or transfer to CID, were submitted to the Commissioner of Police, Nizamabad (complaints dated 24.02.2026 and 02.03.2026), the District Collector & Magistrate, Nizamabad, the Director General of Police (DGP), Telangana, the State Public Prosecutor at the Telangana High Court (representation dated 06.04.2026), and the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC, New Delhi, complaint dated 22.03.2026).

Far from ensuring an independent investigation, the local police doubled down on intimidation. On April 23, 2026, the victim’s grieving husband, Devidas, was unlawfully detained at the Nandipet Police Station for hours solely to coerce him into signing statements forgiving the landlord. The Investigating Officer categorically refused to record his supplementary statement under Section 161 CrPC.

A formal complaint was also placed before the Telangana State Police Complaints Authority (SPCA), Hyderabad. Initially, the SPCA had issued notices and reminder memos directing the Commissioner of Police, Nizamabad, to conduct an inquiry and submit a comprehensive report. However, on September 1, 2026, the Chairman of the State Police Complaints Authority, Justice Dr. B. Siva Sankara Rao (Retired High Court Judge), issued final proceedings (Proceedings C.No. 116/S1/SPCA/2026). Accepting at face value the enquiry report submitted by the Commissioner of Police, Nizamabad (Letter C.No. G1/267-271-329/CPO-NZB/(SPCA)/2026 dated 31.08.2026), the Authority summarily closed the matter.

The SPCA order stated that the enquiry report clearly disclosed suicide by the deceased, dismissed the family’s suspicions of gang-rape and murder as being “with no basis,” and ruled that there was no basis to take cognizance against any police personnel. By rubber-stamping the self-exonerating report of the very police commissionerate accused of shielding upper-caste suspects, the statutory complaint mechanism effectively shut its doors on the family, sanctifying the police cover-up under legal finality.

Compounding this injustice, the bereaved family of Late Rekha Waghmare is still left wandering from pillar to post, roaming around police stations and administrative offices just to obtain a copy of the enquiry report that was allegedly submitted to the Police Complaints Authority. In a blatant display of institutional non-transparency and high-handedness, neither the State Police Complaints Authority nor the district police authorities have furnished a copy of this vital enquiry report to the family. The victim’s husband and relatives are forced to knock on official doors repeatedly, only to be turned away, denied access to the very document that was used behind closed doors to dismiss their plea and whitewash the grave allegations of sexual violence and murder.

The Hypocrisy Laid Bare: Caste Society Masquerading as Civil Society

The simultaneous timelines of these two cases lay bare the systemic fault lines of Telangana’s public sphere. In the Miss X case, an allegation involving influential families provoked an immediate, coordinated reaction: high-decibel street protests, relentless television debates, dharnas outside police directorates, and interventions by mainstream women’s organisations. That sustained public outcry gave the police no room to compromise, forcing an arrest and custodial interrogation within days.

In stark and shameful contrast, the alleged gang-rape and murder of Late Rekha Waghmare, a destitute Dalit migrant mother whose body carried an 8 x 4 cm scalp contusion and subdural brain hemorrhage, was met with complete, deafening silence. On April 3, 2026, an online petition was initiated and circulated across social media platforms, WhatsApp groups, Facebook, and X (formerly Twitter). Yet not a single mainstream political party held a dharna. Not a single prominent feminist forum marched through the streets of Hyderabad or Nizamabad. The civil society organisations that claim to stand for democratic rights stayed comfortably silent.

Even more disheartening is that Ambedkarite and Dalit organizations also failed to take up this grave issue for reasons known only to them. Because Rekha Waghmare was merely an impoverished, landless migrant laborer, her brutal death offered neither immediate political mileage nor high-profile visibility. It was neither a prominent electoral issue nor a fight over the promotion or bureaucratic posting of an influential Scheduled Caste officer, matters that often galvanize Dalit and employee associations into vociferous agitations and press conferences. Her utter lack of socio-economic capital and political utility rendered her invisible even to those claiming to safeguard Dalit rights, proving that institutional apathy is compounded by internal indifference when the victim is a powerless, working-class woman from the margins.

Why this disparity? The answer lies in the harsh reality of social power. When a victim belongs to an influential or socially dominant stratum, society identifies with her victimhood, and outrage becomes a currency of civic duty and political advantage. But when the victim is a Dalit woman, an “untouchable” migrant labourer from another state whose alleged killers are local landed elites, the calculations collapse into indifference. The police feel no pressure from civil society, the administration faces no electoral threat, and oversight institutions like the Police Complaints Authority effortlessly dismiss grave forensic trauma based on one-sided, concealed police memos.

Conclusion: A Call for Reckoning and Justice

A genuine civil society cannot operate on selective empathy. When human rights defenders, feminists, and political platforms extend their solidarity only to privileged victims while abandoning Dalit women to systemic state violence and police collusion, they cease to function as a civil society; they function as an entrenched caste society.

The Telangana Police Complaints Authority’s summary closure of the complaint on September 1, 2026, and its refusal to even provide the family with the inquiry report, is not the end of this struggle; it indicts an entire system. Justice for Late Rekha Waghmare requires immediate judicial intervention, an independent Special Investigation Team probe uncompromised by local influence, the alteration of FIR No. 33/2026 to include murder and gang-rape charges under the BNS and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, and stringent accountability for the police officers who fabricated statements, suppressed forensic evidence, and concealed inquiry records. As long as the people and leaders of Telangana ignore the crimes committed against poor and powerless communities, their boast of being a modern, fair, and progressive society is just a fake front.

Dr. B. Karthik Navayan, Advocate and Human Rights Activist

author: rti_admin
title: The Ahmedabad Reading Controversy and the Freedom to Read
content:
Who gets to decide what we should read? The question arose sharply in Ahmedabad this August, when two books were removed from a school reading list, and a silent reading session was later disrupted.

In August, an Ahmedabad school removed Malala Yousafzai’s I Am Malala and Anne Frank’s The Diary of a Young Girl from its reading list after objections from some parents and protests involving right-wing organisations. Later that month, a silent reading session organised in Vastrapur was reportedly disrupted by a group claiming affiliation with the Vishwa Hindu Parishad and Bajrang Dal. The gathering included students, lawyers, media professionals and others. The reading itself became the object of confrontation.

I Am Malala is the memoir of a girl who survived an assassination attempt after publicly advocating girls’ right to education. The Diary of a Young Girl records the experiences of a Jewish teenager hiding from Nazi persecution before Anne Frank died during the Holocaust. Whatever one thinks of Malala’s political views, or of the ways her story is interpreted, reading her memoir does not require accepting every view she holds. Anne Frank’s diary similarly allows readers to encounter the testimony of a young person caught inside one of history’s greatest crimes.

A book is not a political membership card.

Reading allows a person to encounter an argument without accepting it. A reader can examine its evidence, question its assumptions and reject its conclusions. The point is that judgement becomes possible through encounter.

Education is often described as the transmission of knowledge. But knowledge without the capacity to question it can become another form of conformity.

This question of who may read and what they may encounter carries a specific weight in the Indian context. For much of India’s history, access to formal education was deeply shaped by caste hierarchy. Ambedkar wrote that under the Chaturvarna system, the right to education was assigned to the Brahmins, Kshatriyas and Vaishyas, while Shudras were denied it. He also discussed the denial of education to women. The control of education was therefore connected to the wider system of graded inequality that Ambedkar analysed.

This was one of the structures challenged by Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule. Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, and Phule later set up schools for the Mahars and Mangs. In his 1882 testimony before the Education Commission, Phule criticised the concentration of education among the higher classes and called for a wider spread of primary and female education. His educational work treated access to knowledge as a social question rather than a privilege confined to a small section of society.

Dr B.R. Ambedkar’s conception of democracy makes this problem especially important. In Annihilation of Caste, he imagined an ideal society with “varied and free points of contact with other modes of association” and described democracy as “a mode of associated living.” For Ambedkar, fraternity was not sameness. It required people to participate in a common social world despite their differences. His writings on the Depressed Classes emerged from a context in which these communities faced restrictions on access to public wells and schools, and were subjected to social segregation and prescribed occupations. The “associated living” he imagined presupposes that those who were once excluded from classrooms are now full participants in the world of ideas.

A democratic society cannot expect citizens to form independent judgements while continually narrowing the range of ideas they are permitted to encounter. The democratic reader needs the freedom to examine an argument before deciding whether it deserves acceptance, rejection or further examination.

John Dewey understood education as inseparable from democratic life. For Dewey, democracy depended on communication, inquiry and shared experience. He saw education as a way of preparing people to participate intelligently in common life.

Not every book belongs in every classroom. Parents can question reading lists, teachers can challenge texts, and schools can make decisions about age, pedagogy and context. Citizens can protest. A democratic society must leave room for disagreement over education. The important distinction is between arguing that a book should not be taught and intimidating people who choose to read it. The first concerns the content and place of a text in education. The second makes the act of reading itself a political offence.

Contemporary concerns about caste discrimination in higher education, including its relationship to student distress and suicides, remain serious enough to have been examined by the Supreme Court-appointed National Task Force on student mental health and suicides.

The harder democratic principle is to defend the reader’s freedom even when we dislike the book being read. Otherwise, “intellectual freedom” simply becomes another name for allowing ideas with which we already agree.

This is why the Ahmedabad episode matters beyond the two books involved. The deeper question is who gets to decide what a citizen may encounter before that citizen has had the opportunity to form a judgement.

Once reading itself becomes evidence of political allegiance, we begin judging the person who has chosen to read a book rather than only the ideas within it. “What does this book say?” becomes “What does reading this book say about you?” The reader is then placed on trial alongside the ideas in the book.

A society that makes the second question more important than the first risks producing citizens who know which ideas belong to their side but have little opportunity to examine ideas outside that boundary.

The people who gathered for the silent reading session in Vastrapur had come to read. They were exercising their judgement through the simple act of sitting with books.

A democratic citizen should be free to encounter an idea, question it, and decide what to make of it. In India, defending that freedom is inseparable from defending the right of readers from the Depressed Classes and other communities historically excluded from education to full and equal access to the world of texts.

Rajat Kanti Satpati is an author of several books. His writing has appeared in SteinbeckNow, People’s Daily, and other publications.

author: rti_admin
title: The Questions of Milinda: Publisher’s Note on Navayana Edition
content:
A river remains alive only so long as fresh water continues to flow through it. The same principle applies to language. Language is never static; it evolves with time. Its vocabulary, sentence structure, and modes of expression continually change. Whether one considers Hindi, English, or any other language, it becomes evident that literature written in the nineteenth century is often difficult for contemporary readers to approach without assistance.

For this reason, responsible publishers of classical literature frequently present ancient works in a renewed form, adapting their language, style, and presentation to the needs of modern readers. Such efforts enable timeless ideas to remain accessible to new generations.

When we turn to Buddhist literature, however, we find that relatively little attention has been given to this task. Many texts continue to be published in styles that remain largely unchanged from earlier translations. Regrettably, this has contributed to an increasing distance between younger readers and the rich intellectual heritage of Buddhism.

One remarkable work that has suffered from this situation is the Milinda Pañha (Questions of King Milinda). This extraordinary text preserves a series of profound dialogues between King Milinda and Venerable Nāgasena, offering readers an accessible gateway into the heart of Buddhist philosophy through reasoned inquiry and debate.

Today, this book can be found in many Buddhist households across India. Yet experience suggests that, although it occupies a place of honour on many bookshelves, it is seldom read in its entirety. Many readers begin it with enthusiasm but fail to complete it. This is not mere excuse-making; it is a practical reality. The difficulty arises largely from an archaic style of translation and a language that often feels distant from contemporary readers.

As publishers, we felt it insufficient merely to lament this situation. Instead, we resolved to seek a constructive solution. Our volume, The Questions of Milinda: Milindapañha in Navayana Perspective, represents the second step in that endeavour. The first was Navayāna Darśana: A Modern Interpretation of the Buddha’s Teachings, which presented Buddhist philosophy in a simple, rational, and contemporary style. The enthusiastic response it received, leading it nearly to go out of print, encouraged us to continue this work.

The present book is not a direct translation of the original Pāli text. Rather, it is a careful reworking based upon a comparative study of English, Hindi, and, to some extent, Marathi translations. Many existing versions contain accounts of previous births and other traditional elements that appear difficult to reconcile with modern scientific understanding and with claims concerning the rational and humanistic character of Buddhist philosophy.

In this edition, Author Ratnesh Katulkar has sought to remove such accretions and reinterpret the text through a Navayāna perspective, presenting it in a clear, modern, and accessible form for contemporary readers. Yet this undertaking presented a significant challenge. The original questions of Milinda and the replies of Nāgasena could neither be arbitrarily expanded nor fundamentally altered. How, then, could they be made more approachable?

The solution adopted was both simple and effective. The original dialogues have been preserved with only minimal modifications, mainly involving language and presentation. However, following nearly every question-and-answer exchange, explanatory sections have been added in which the discussion is interpreted afresh in the light of modern knowledge and contemporary concerns. In this way, the text has been connected to present realities while preserving the spirit of the original dialogue.

We are confident that this approach will appeal both to readers already interested in Buddhist philosophy and to newcomers seeking an accessible introduction to the Dhamma.

It is only natural, however, that some readers deeply attached to traditional interpretations and inherited assumptions may not feel entirely comfortable with this presentation. Any attempt to revisit established traditions is often met with resistance. Yet the Buddha’s path itself is one of inquiry, reflection, and continuous investigation. Following the spirit of the Kālāma Sutta, it encourages individuals to examine truth for themselves rather than accept doctrines solely based on authority or tradition.

Our purpose is not to provoke those committed to conventional views, but to ensure that younger generations become active participants in the Buddhist intellectual heritage. For that reason, it is perhaps best to pay little attention to reactionary criticism. Navayāna, after all, resembles an elephant that continues steadily on its path without being distracted by passing noises. This book is simply another step in that journey.

History repeatedly demonstrates that every significant intellectual and social transformation faced opposition in its own time. Yet it is often these very transformations that later shape the course of human civilisation. Generations afterwards, historians frequently look back with surprise at the resistance such movements encountered.

Navayāna is part of that continuing tradition of renewal. The flame first kindled by the Buddha illuminated vast regions of the world in the age of Emperor Aśoka. Though dimmed during periods of decline and reaction, it was rekindled in modern times by figures such as P. Lakshmi Narasu, Dharmanand Kosambi, and Dr B. R. Ambedkar, inspiring countless thinkers and reformers across the world. Each of these individuals encountered hostility from conservative circles; therefore, criticism of our own efforts should come as no surprise. Indeed, our author often remarks that a positive mind can transform even hostility and irritation into a source of strength and motivation.

This book was not written in isolation. The entire manuscript was taught and discussed online with students over an extended period. Every dialogue, criticism, observation, and suggestion emerging from those discussions was carefully considered and incorporated where appropriate. The final text was subsequently reviewed and approved by the wider Navayāna study group. Consequently, this volume should not be viewed merely as the private opinion of its author. It is, rather, a collective expression shaped through dialogue, study, reflection, and collaboration among the students of Navayāna. We sincerely hope that readers will find it worthy of their expectations.

We humbly request all readers to share their reflections, suggestions, and critical assessments after reading this book. Your thoughtful responses will guide and inspire our future work.

Book Title: The Questions of Milinda: Milindapañha in Navayana Perspective

Publisher: Navayana Prakashan, Nasik

author: rti_admin
title: The IITs: Tragic Failures That Beget More Tragedies
content:
From a social perspective, the IITs are tragic failures that beget more tragedies.

But you already know the IITs are the pinnacle of Indian aspirations, achievements, accolades, blah-di-blah, right? How about we celebrate by taking a closer look at the graduates, the faculty, and the institution?

The institutional charter, briefly. The IITs were conceived in 1946 to support the country’s industrial development and help meet the nation’s technological challenges. Parliament’s 1961 Act declares them institutions of national importance. It charges them with instruction and research, and with the advancement of learning and dissemination of knowledge. The same Act says every institute shall be open to persons of either sex and of whatever race, creed, caste or class, in admitting or appointing students and teachers alike. [1] Later laws reserve seats for SC, ST and OBC students, PhD seats included, and, since 2019, teaching posts at every rank.

Start with the product. As any IIT alum would confirm, a majority of IIT graduates wouldn’t be able to properly describe what ‘engineering’ is. title: No, not the Generation: Political Mobilisation and Changing Grammar of Protest in India
content:
Both academic and non-academic spheres are recurrently using terms like “Gen-Z protest,” “Gen Z’s political anger,” “Gen Z pressure,” “Gen-Z consciousness,” and “Gen Z politics” to describe the follow-up events. US public broadcaster NPR, despite accentuating the statistics of joblessness and inequality across South Asia as latent sources of unrest, concludes its argument by portraying “Gen Z” as an active political force. I feel some edginess with how a demographic detail is so readily treated as an explanation, when it is, at best, merely a description. Young people marching in large numbers, staging sit-ins, occupying public spaces, and facing tear gas are not new phenomena of 2026. These have long been a persistent feature of political activism in India. For instance, Bhagat Singh’s Naujawan Bharat Sabha (1926) had already demonstrated the political mobilization of youth nearly a century before.

Protests against exam-leaks are not new to India. We witnessed similar protests regarding the NEET exam in 2024. However, in 2026 the movement evolved into a mass youth mobilization, garnering national and international attention. It was driver not solely due to the examination scandal, but its collision with an unrelated event.
